r.title: Cataloguing the case of the clay seals
paragraphs: A. A fictional museum faced an awkward problem when it prepared a small exhibition from the estate of a former collector. The largest box held ninety clay seals attributed to an old riverside market. An early accession record described the gift as 'complete', an adjective interpreted by the first exhibition designer to mean that the objects represented the market as a whole. The surviving packing sheets gave a different impression. One listed objects selected to travel abroad, while another listed damaged seals that had remained in a local store. The museum revised its label to say that it held a selection of objects from the site, rather than a representative set.

B. A researcher then noticed that the seals carried numbers in two styles of handwriting. The numbers ending in a letter matched a set of photographs from the year of excavation. The plain numbers had been added much later when the collector rearranged the objects by size. Treating every number as an original field reference would therefore have linked several seals to the wrong position in the market. The museum did not remove the later labels. It entered both systems in the database, adding a field that explained whether a number described an original find or a later place in a collection.

C. Identifying the relevant people outside the museum proved more difficult than reconstructing the numbering. The site was just beyond the present boundary of a growing town. A neighbouring community had long maintained its riverside paths and had gathered family accounts of earlier work on the land. A first public meeting was held in the town hall, but the organisers later repeated it in the village after several interested residents said they had not received the invitation. The museum offered to pay travel expenses for the second round of consultations and translated its evidence list into the region's two most widely used languages.

D. The final agreement kept responsibility for treatment with the museum laboratory for a fixed period and assigned decisions on public display to a panel including representatives chosen by both communities. Instead of proposing that the museum produce a single final interpretation, the panel asked it to distinguish claims supported by material records from interpretations based on later interviews. New evidence could be added without silently rewriting earlier entries. The exhibition materials were revised to indicate which statements still depended on assumptions. By the time the first batch of seals returned from the laboratory, the objects had fuller catalogue entries and there was a clearer account of which conclusions the evidence could support.

Today I want to explain three steps a campus museum can take when it finds two documents for the same object. I will use an example from our practice collection: a small wooden model of a gate. The collection number is on a paper tag, while an older number survives in pencil underneath the base. The temptation is to select one number and discard the other. Before doing that, consider what each identifier was meant to record.
A

First, photograph the object from all sides before moving its tag. Don't just photograph the underside where the pencil is. We need a record of the condition of the whole model, including small breaks near the gate itself. Those breaks can help match it with photographs from earlier years. When you make your first comparison, use the edge of the base rather than its colour. Oxidation can change the colour of exposed wood, but an uneven edge is likely to be visible in both pictures.
A

Second, look at the source of each number. During last year's workshop, a student called her paper tag a field label. An old inventory showed, however, that staff had made the paper label for a sale that never took place. The pencil number was associated with a repair invoice. Both were valuable, but neither could establish where the model was found. Only the archive clerk's packing list described its origin.
A

Third, write your conclusion under the label 'provisional'. In this exercise, I prefer a provisional comment to an entry marked 'unknown', because you have established what the numbers do refer to. Use dates if they are supported by the paperwork. If a new document arrives, append an update rather than deleting your initial note. This will let the next person see which piece of evidence changed your account. For next week, each of you will submit a photograph, a one-page comparison and a short paragraph explaining how certain you are. I am not asking for a video this time.

w: Academic Task 1

The chart shows two U.S. Census measures in 2010 and 2020: the number of multigenerational households and the number of children under 18 living in a grandparent’s home. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Start with the shared increase, then compare the magnitude of change. Keep the unit clear within each category. Avoid adding the figures or using either one as a percentage of the other. The displayed numbers are rounded to the nearest tenth of a million.

Both measures were higher in 2020 than in 2010. The number of multigenerational households rose from 5.1 million to 6.0 million, an increase of about 0.9 million. The gap between the two displayed figures narrowed from 0.7 million to 0.1 million. These are separate counts with different units, so the comparison describes the numerical change in each measure rather than the share of children living in multigenerational households.

r.title: One roof, two front doors
paragraphs: A. The fictional housing association of Pearbank received two apparently contradictory requests when it asked members what kind of homes should be built beside the old bus garage. Older applicants often asked to live closer to their children and grandchildren, while the younger households said they wanted clearer boundaries around home life. The architects had begun with the assumption that sharing a building required sharing kitchens, halls and storage areas. They were prompted to reconsider by a family that wanted the convenience of living next door without feeling that a relative's front door was also their own.

B. The plans therefore paired an ordinary flat with a compact neighbouring flat. The two front doors led to a single landing, and a narrow communal cupboard could hold a pushchair or folding trolley. The rooms on opposite sides of the dividing wall were both bathrooms, rather than bedrooms. The engineers claimed this would reduce the risk that conversations and televisions on one side would interrupt sleep on the other. The first draft also included an internal connecting door. After a workshop with prospective residents, the association decided to offer it only as an option because some people feared that an unused door might still make them feel under pressure to be available.

C. The applicant interviews brought a second problem into focus. Families volunteered to share responsibilities, but they did not always agree on what that meant. Some relatives expected to handle occasional deliveries or lend a tool, while others imagined daily transport and regular childcare. Before accepting an offer, households were asked to discuss what help they thought they could provide, when they would need advance notice and how they might change the arrangement later. The association did not require a weekly commitment of a particular number of hours. It wanted tenants to make arrangements based on their own routines, without losing eligibility if they could not offer more care.

D. Six months after occupancy, the association compared its new pairs of flats with a nearby block of conventional apartments. Applicants for the new homes had signed up partly because they valued frequent contact, so the association cautioned against attributing every difference to the design. The review nevertheless highlighted one detail that came directly from the layout. Several residents said they usually carried shopping and luggage through their own front entrances, but could still see a neighbour's light from the landing or notice a delivered parcel. In the final report this form of small-scale contact mattered more to residents than the internal connecting doors. Only three households had chosen to install them.

l.title: Designing a housing follow-up study
lines: A
For our module project, I'd like to examine two blocks whose residents share courtyards. My first idea was to find out whether people spoke to one another more often near the largest courtyard.
B

The project tutor said size was not our main issue. She suggested we compare how people arrive home. Some take a route that passes the courtyard every day; others reach their flats by a side stair. We can see what difference that makes even when the courtyard stays the same.
A

Right. We should keep the observation schedule comparable. I was thinking of recording at eight in the morning, but the entry office told me a lot of residents are already out by then. Could we start at six in the evening, when people return from work?
B

Yes. Let's observe on Thursday, then repeat on Saturday. A Saturday morning would give very different conditions, though. I think we should keep both sessions at six o'clock. We can record how often someone pauses to talk, but we shouldn't note what they say.
A
Good point. The activity sheet includes a question about names. We don't need names at all. We can write an apartment number on the sheet, or would that identify someone?
B

It might. Why not use a letter for each route instead? Each time someone comes through the gate, add a mark in the right column. When a visitor isn't clearly a resident, record just the route, not their purpose.
A

For the interview, we can contact the residents' group first. I wanted to ask the building manager to recruit people, but the tutor was concerned that only the households already in contact with the manager would get an invitation. The residents' group offered to display a message by the lift and give everyone a chance to reply.
B
We should bring the draft to Tuesday's seminar, including an example of the chart we will use. The observation results won't be ready, of course. The point is to show how we'd plot the two routes.

w: Task 2 · Problem and solution

People who provide unpaid care for relatives often find it difficult to take time away from this responsibility. What problems does this cause, and what could employers and local authorities do to help?

Choose two concrete problems and trace each back to difficulty taking a break. A missed training course and unreliable appointments belong to different chains of cause and effect. Let employers and authorities respond to the constraints each can actually control.

A worker who needs to be home at a fixed time may turn down training if the course runs unpredictably, even when the employer nominally offers equal access. A manager could send out start and finish times early and give workers a written procedure for swapping equivalent shifts. A short public respite service would address a different problem: a worker may still need someone to cover the scheduled break, for example during an evening appointment. A trial could track whether participants were able to keep their commitments and how often a replacement fell through.

r.title: The value of a place that stays empty
paragraphs: A. In the fictional district of Ryecombe a respite service lent trained staff to households whose members normally provided unpaid care. The manager wanted to extend the service beyond planned hours, because some applicants needed replacement care when a hospital appointment or school meeting appeared suddenly. A proposed trial kept one member of staff free until noon each weekday to cover bookings made that morning. When the first monthly report showed that some standby hours had passed without a visit, an administrator proposed selling the morning slots as ordinary appointments. The service could fill more hours and cancel fewer visits on paper, but would then have little capacity to respond quickly.

B. The manager asked two households to keep diaries so that the service could observe what happened before a call. One household had booked respite far in advance, but its carer had missed several ordinary appointments because it was hard to predict the exact day when help would be needed. The second household had only made three calls in a month, yet its carer kept two medical appointments that she would have cancelled without knowing standby help was available. In the following month, the service invited fifteen more households to keep the same record. The participants were told they could record a reason as 'private' without explaining why they had asked for help.

C. Early results raised an issue of fairness. Households calling as soon as the office opened were the most likely to obtain a standby slot. One group of carers usually completed a morning school run before they could make a telephone call and therefore missed several opportunities. The office added a short window for text requests and grouped together submissions received before ten o'clock. Staff then prioritised time-sensitive needs and used a rotating list if two requests were equally urgent. They did not guarantee an appointment to everyone who used the text route, but they made the timing and priority procedure available in advance.

D. The final report counted used standby hours and published a different measure alongside that figure: the proportion of people who reported keeping a specific commitment because they could arrange cover at short notice. The service also noted where a time-sensitive request had gone unfilled. It did not call an hour successful merely because staff were waiting, or unsuccessful solely because a household had no reason to use it on that day. Its recommendation was to choose the amount of standby capacity by balancing the consequences of missed requests against the cost of keeping skilled staff free.

l.title: A call about covering an evening shift
lines: A
Respite booking service. This is Robin speaking.
B

Hello. I'm trying to book a visit so I can attend a training session on Monday. I think I registered under the name Avery Grant. Last month I had cover from six until eight, but the new session starts earlier.
A
I have your registration. The record says Park Lane. Is that still your address?
B

We moved from Park Lane last month. The address to use now is Flat 8, number 72, Willow Street. The entrance is near the post office. If the volunteer comes by bus, the closest stop is by the chemist.
A
Thanks. Monday's early slots are difficult. There is a visit open from five fifteen to seven fifteen. Alternatively, Tuesday starts at half past four. Does Monday's slot give you enough time?
B

Monday is essential because that's the only session where I can submit the forms. Five fifteen is all right: once I get on the tram, the training centre is a ten-minute ride. The bus takes twenty-five minutes, which would be too slow.
A

Then Monday at five fifteen. The service charge for two hours is twelve pounds. If you were using the new room at our centre it would cost eight, but this is a home visit. You'll receive an invoice, so you won't need to pay the person who arrives.
B
Good. Do I need to leave instructions? My sister will be there at the start and can introduce everyone. She has a card with the usual routine. I can also email it.
A

Please hand the card to the volunteer directly rather than email personal details. Let them know which neighbour to contact if your sister has to go and the volunteer needs help getting into the downstairs hallway. A reminder will come by text on Sunday. To confirm, just reply by noon that day. For cancellations, please ring the office. We only read replies marked 'confirm' on Sunday.
B
Fine. Thanks for sorting it out.
